A1-A2.headline: Battle of the Sexes in Tennis

pages.text: The term Battle of the Sexes describes tennis matches played between men and women. The most famous match happened in 1973. A 55-year-old man named Bobby Riggs played against a 29-year-old woman named Billie Jean King. They played at the Houston Astrodome. Millions of people watched the game on television.

Before playing King, Bobby Riggs played against Margaret Court in May 1973. Riggs had been a top male player in the 1940s. Court was a top female player. Riggs used drop shots and lobs to win the match quickly in two sets. His victory landed him on the cover of magazines.

After beating Court, Riggs challenged all female tennis players. This prompted Billie Jean King to play against him in a prime time match. The game had a large prize of one hundred thousand dollars. It took place on September 20, 1973, in Texas.

Billie Jean King won the match against Riggs in three sets. She believed winning was very important for women's tennis and for women's rights. She thought losing the match would set women's sports back many years. Her victory became a major milestone in public acceptance.

Other similar matches took place over the years. In 1992, Jimmy Connors played Martina Navratilova in a match called the Battle of Champions. Connors won that game. At least eight other exhibition matches have been played between male and female tennis players starting back in 1888.

B1-B2.headline: The History of Battle of the Sexes Tennis Matches

pages.text: In tennis, the phrase Battle of the Sexes refers to exhibition matches played between men and women. The most famous encounter took place in 1973 at the Houston Astrodome, where 55-year-old Bobby Riggs faced 29-year-old Billie Jean King. An estimated fifty million people in the United States watched King win in three sets.

Four months prior, Riggs played Margaret Court in Ramona, California. Riggs, a former top player and master promoter, claimed he could still beat top female players. Using drop shots and lobs, Riggs defeated Court easily in two sets. The quick defeat was dubbed the Mother's Day Massacre by media outlets.

Emboldened by his win, Riggs taunted female players, leading Billie Jean King to accept a high-stakes match in prime time. Promoted as the Battle of the Sexes, the event offered a winner-takes-all prize of one hundred thousand dollars. Before the broadcast, King issued an ultimatum to remove commentator Jack Kramer.

King ultimately defeated Riggs in three sets before a massive television audience. She viewed the match as crucial for the women's liberation movement and women's tennis, believing a loss would severely damage female self-esteem. Her victory is widely considered a major milestone in sports history.

Other notable matchups occurred in later years. In 1992, Jimmy Connors and Martina Navratilova played under hybrid rules in a match dubbed The Battle of Champions, which Connors won. Additionally, various exhibition matches between male and female players have occurred since 1888, featuring players like Lottie Dod and Bill Tilden.

Decades later, discussions around these events continue to surface. Some speculation arose regarding whether Riggs intentionally lost his match against King due to gambling debts, though King firmly rejected those claims. Other players, like Navratilova, attributed Riggs's loss simply to his advanced age of 55.

C1-C2.headline: An Overview of Historical Battle of the Sexes Matches

pages.text: The designation Battle of the Sexes describes exhibition matches contested between male and female tennis players. The most prominent instance occurred in 1973 at the Houston Astrodome between 55-year-old Bobby Riggs and 29-year-old Billie Jean King. King secured victory in three sets during an event broadcast to tens of millions worldwide, marking a significant milestone for women's tennis.

Four months earlier, Riggs faced Margaret Court in a match arranged after Riggs asserted his superiority over contemporary female players. Utilizing strategic drop shots and lobs, Riggs defeated Court in straight sets. The swift defeat prompted widespread media attention and earned the moniker of the Mother's Day Massacre.

Following his victory over Court, Riggs's continued taunts induced King to accept a lucrative, nationally televised challenge in prime time. Prior to the broadcast, King successfully demanded the removal of commentator Jack Kramer to deny him a platform to disparage women's tennis, ensuring her participation in the high-stakes event.

King regarded the contest as a critical pivot point for sexual equality and the women's liberation movement, driven by the conviction that defeat would severely impede public acceptance of women's athletics. Her subsequent triumph fulfilled these cultural stakes, cementing the match's legacy in sports history.

Subsequent years saw additional iterations of intergender competition. In 1992, Jimmy Connors and Martina Navratilova contested the Battle of Champions under hybrid rules favoring the female player, resulting in a victory for Connors. Historical records indicate at least eight prior exhibitions dating back to 1888 involving notable champions under various handicaps.

Later historical analyses introduced various perspectives on the outcomes. Speculation regarding possible match-fixing involving gambling debts surfaced decades later through investigative reporting, though King adamantly dismissed suggestions that Riggs tanked the match. Other athletes, including Navratilova, attributed Riggs's defeat primarily to his age.
